analytic.title: Optimizing QoS in Adaptive Real-Time Systems with Energy Constraint Varying CPU Frequency

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The life time of some real-time systems is determined by batteries, thus necessitating a mechanism for energy management. These systems must consider not only schedulability constraints to ensure temporal correctness but also their energy limitations to accomplish their considered mission. Moreover, it is still desired that the system provides services with the best possible quality. This work presents a problem of selecting the frequency for each task to fulfill the system goal, while considering issues of schedulability and energy consumption. The problem is formulated in mathematical programming and solved with a convexoptimization algorithm. It is assumed that CPU frequency can be selected continuously within a given range. The system reconfiguration scheme assumes the earliest deadline first (EDF) policy, with soft and hard real-time tasks managed by some bandwidth reservation scheme. The effectiveness of the proposed solution is shown through numerical analysis.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The number of embedded systems that rely on batteries to operate is increasing steadily, in particular robots, mobile phones, and tablets. These systems are found in many applications, ranging from entertainment to critical missions, such as the BigDog robot which is capable of making decisions in unstructured environments (environmental conditions can't be determined beforehand) and carrying out missions that can endanger human life [1].

The complexity of such systems grows according with their functionality, as they require more accurate model and more computational power. With complexity comes more energy consumption, which implies a shorter time of operation, as in the case of the robot Pioneer 3-DX where uptime decreases around 50% when the embedded computer is activated [2]. Consequently, it becomes necessary to implement mechanisms for power management, which should ensure enough battery life to finish the mission.

This work provides a mechanism to dynamically select the frequency of the CPU to run tasks considering restrictions of scalability and energy availability. Our proposed mechanism takes into account a scenario where the computational load of the tasks is not constant, but rather varies dynamically over time. Therefore, there arises the need to adjust the frequency according to the time required to accomplish the mission, the CPU load, and the available energy. The variation of the CPU utilization of the tasks is related to external events. Despite the complexity of the problem, we found a convex-optimization formulation, for which highly efficient algorithms can be applied. In this context, in this paper we: provide a detailed analysis of energy functions; derive a convex formulation for the problem; solve the derived problem via an efficient optimization method; and evaluate the proposed solution via numerical analysis.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II discusses related work. Section III presents the task and energy model. Section IV develops a convexprogramming formulation for the task reconfiguration mechanism. Section V delineates an interior-point method for solving the reconfiguration problems. Section VI reports the results from a numerical analysis. Finally, Section VII offers some conclusions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) is a technique commonly used to achieve energy savings in real-time systems. In [3], experiments were performed with a video application, which proves the potential of energy saving when using DVFS, although the technique does not consider energy devices besides the CPU.

In [4], it was shown that in some cases decreasing frequency can actually increase energy consumption, rather than the opposite as would be expected. In [5], it was performed an analysis of energy consumption considering CPU and other devices used by the system tasks. Based on that, a dynamic power management (DPM) technique uses DVFS, considering other components used by a task besides the CPU [6].

The problem addressed in [7], [8] seeks to minimize energy consumption with on-line algorithms that take advantage of processor idle time. These works differ from ours in that they use best effort techniques and consider only hard real-time tasks (HRT), whereas our proposal focuses on a solution that runs on-line, provides guarantees on energy economy, and admits HRT and soft real-time (SRT) tasks.

Other works like [8] apply optimization off-line to calculate a minimum frequency that a task should run to induce the least energy consumption rate. Again, they consider only HRT tasks and no guarantees of energy consumption are provided. In some systems that accomplish missions like robots, it is necessary to ensure a minimum energy save keeping the quality of its provided services as high as possible. Thus, there arises the need to provide a guarantee of quality of service (QoS) and minimal energy-savings.

We propose a mechanism as [9], [10], that can be solved on-line, taking both SRT and HRT tasks into consideration, while saving energy and avoiding system QoS degradation. Our model considers the importance that each task has for the system. The aim is to manage energy consumption by adjusting CPU frequency so that the system finishes its mission with the maximum possible QoS, that should reduce the risk of a SRT task missing the deadline according with its importance to the system.

div.head: III. MODEL
div.p: Models for real-time system task and energy consumption are presented herein.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: In general the system considered for this work consists of a set of n independent SRT or HRT tasks that share a single processor, which can run in a continuous range of CPU frequency. If τ i is a HRT task it is assumed that its worst-case execution time, at maximum frequency and including the devices operations, C i and its period T i are known. These parameters for SRT tasks are assumed to represent their average behavior. Temporal isolation between tasks in the system is ensured by a bandwidth reservation mechanism such as CBS [11]. This is necessary to avoid that overruns of a task interfere in the execution for the others. Each task τ i is executed by a server S i and there is a server for each task. Server S i is defined by a tuple (Q i , T i ), meaning that τ i may use up to Q i time units within T i . It is further assumed that servers are scheduled by EDF and server periods are the same as the period of the tasks they serve.

The budget Q i is defined in terms of Q D i and Q I i , which represent the time an instance of τ i may spend using CPU and other devices, respectively. The budget Q D i is considered to be inversely proportional to the value of the selected frequency (e.g. Q D i increases by 100% when the processor frequency is reduced by 50%). As Q I i depends on the use of other resources such as memory and hard drive, it is independent of the chosen frequency. Thus, the total budget of S i is expressed in terms of the budgets and the frequency f i of the CPU as
div.formula: Q i = Q D i fi + Q I i .
div.p: Processor utilization is determined by the sum of the utilization of each server S i , which is calculated by
div.formula: u i = Qi Ti = Q I i Ti + Q D i
div.p: Tifi . Thus, for the tasks to be EDF-schedulable the n i=1 u i ≤ 1 condition must hold. Since choosing a new frequency for a set of tasks consumes CPU resources, a management algorithm should be invoked only when needed.

A profit should be associated with each S i for the correct application of the model, which must take into consideration the characteristics and purpose of the system, because it represents how advantageous is to execute a task in a specific frequency. The induced profit must capture its importance for the system: its processor demand in terms of CPU utilization, and the effect of degradation caused for the system. The importance of a task τ i is applicationdependent and must be assigned by the system designer or decided by the system on execution time. For this, we define a parameter α i to represent the relative importance of τ i in the system. That is, we assume that the profit associated to τ i is a function of α i , the utilization u i , and the selected frequency f i . We postpone further discussion on the considered objective function to Section IV, where the optimization problem is formally defined.

div.head: B. Energy Model
div.p: For the energy model we assume that processor frequency is continuous in a certain interval. This can be achieved, as explained in [12]. Also, we assume that the energy consumption of tasks takes into account the devices they use. The allocated devices are put into sleep mode when a task is not running [13].

We note that the second assumption above is in line with budgets and CPU utilization equations, which takes CPUdependent and CPU independent parameters into account. For energy, we use the DPM model [14], which represents the energy consumption of a task τ i per unit of time:
div.formula: P i = P I i + P D i + P S(1)
div.p: where: P I i is the electric power that is independent of processor frequency (hard drive and other devices), being determined by the devices used by the task τ i ; P D i indicates the power consumed by the CPU to perform a task; P S is the power cost to maintain the system devices in the sleep mode when not in use. P S is a given constant and cannot be modified and as such will be omitted to simplify the developments.
P D i is given by the dynamic power of the processor, for a task τ i , which according to [7] is defined as:
div.formula: P D i = C ef V 2 i F i (2)
div.p: where F i is the frequency used by the processor to perform task τ i , C ef is the capacitance required to execute an instruction, and V i is the voltage needed to operate the system at frequency F i . We use f i = Fi Fmax as normalized frequency for case of representation.

The voltage required for the processor to operate at a frequency f i is given based on the frequency that the CPU operates, namely V i ≈ V max f i [8]. Thus, the CPU power consumption of a task is expressed as
div.formula: P D i = C ef V 2 max f 3 i F max
div.p: and the total system power by a task becomes:

The analysis above indicates that each task has its minimum frequency dependent on which of the three scenarios P i (f i ) falls in. Because the energy consumption of a task is not fixed due to the variability of the computational load, task running time and mode vary according to the environment conditions. Consequently, it is not possible to estimate exactly how much energy will be needed to accomplish a goal. Therefore, it becomes necessary to estimate the economy needed in the worst-case during a certain interval of time, or in response to an event, to avoid more than necessary energy savings which would result in QoS degradation.

div.head: IV. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Given a processor and its operating frequency interval, a value of f min i is determined for task τ i by the analysis explained in the previous section. Under this assumption, the addressed problem consists in choosing the frequencies for a set of tasks that maximize QoS subject to both schedulability and energy constraints. div.p: We now make some comments on the aspects function ( 8) captures. First, we note that according to (8), the reduction in the frequency a task executes implies decreasing its profit. As lower frequencies make running time longer and for soft real-time tasks one is often interested in reducing their response times, this model is suitable. When hard real-time tasks are being considered, however, the issue is mostly related to meeting deadlines. As worst-case execution times of hard tasks are known and constraints (7b) and (7c) ensure system schedulability independently of the selected frequencies, hard tasks can be modeled in function ( 8) by assigning them the smallest values for the importance parameter α i . Further, as function ( 7a) is linear and increasing on f i and all the other terms are given nonnegative constants, it is obviously a convex function given that it consists of a sum of linear functions. Hence, if the remaining nonlinear functions, (7b)-(7d) are convex, then the resulting problem will be convex and, therefore, well-known optimization methods can be applied with the guarantee of finding the globally optimal solution.

To check the convexity of the constraints, it is necessary to calculate the second derivative of the function terms appearing in the sum that defines the constraint function. Then, one has to verify that the second derivative of each of these terms is always nonnegative within the domain of f i . If this happens, then the constraint function is convex because the sum of convex functions is a convex function [16]. By following these steps, one can verify that all of the constraint functions in Problem ( 7) are indeed convex.
So Problem (7) results in an explicit formulation of the (frequency) reconfiguration problem in terms of the task processor frequencies as follows:

div.p: V. INTERIOR-POINT METHOD As the defined reconfiguration Problem ( 9) is convex, it can be solved using the interior-point method which ensures convergence to the global optimum [16]. This method can be seen as a framework for convex problems, whereby the Newton method is applied to a sequence of unconstrained approximations. It is important to mention that the method has a quadratic convergent rate [16].

In order to apply the interior-point method, the problem will be divided in two phases. The first one consists in finding an initial feasible point x, wich should obey all constraints, and the second should use the solution of the first phase to find the optimal solution. Both phases solve a sequence of unconstrained approximation problems. The unconstrained problem is obtained by approximating the constraints in the objective as follows:
div.formula: min g 0 (x) + m i=1 - 1 t log(-g i (x)) (10
div.p: where g 0 is the objective function, g i (x) ≤ 0, i = 1, . . . , m, are the constraints and x = (f i : i = 1, . . . , n). Thus Problem (10) can be efficiently solved with the damped Newton's method [16].

To simplify the notation above, the whole objective function is multiplied by t and the sum is replaced by the barrier function: φ(x) = m i=1 log(-g i (x)). As a result, the unconstrained approximation of Problem (9) becomes:
div.formula: min θ(x) = tg 0 (x) -φ(x) (11a)
div.p: where x ∈ dom θ = {x : g i (x) < 0, i = 1, . . . , m}.

According to [16], although a high value for t implies a better constraint approximation by the logarithmic barrier, the efficiency of the Newton's method decreases due to the ill-conditioning of the Hessian. Instead of solving one problem with a high value of t, the interior-point method solves a sequence of problems (10) for an increasing sequence of values of t, where at each iteration t the optimization of Problem (10) starts from the solution x(t -1) found in the previous iteration, a strategy known as warm start. The interior-point method assumes that the starting solution x(0) is strictly feasible.

Any solution x(t) with t > 0 is unique and is a part of the central path, defined by C = {x(t) : t > 0}. Each solution x(t) is a central point that satisfies the first-order optimality condition ∇θ(x) = 0, which is necessary and also sufficient to ensure that the point x(t) is optimal for Problem (10).

The interior-point method described thus far assumes that a strict feasible starting solution is known to achieve the optimum. In order to find a strict feasible starting point, an arbitrary point x is chosen. If all constraints are satisfied, such an x is taken as an initial solution for the problem. Thus minimizing s to a value below zero provides a means for obtaining the start solution x that strictly obeys all considered constraints. As a result, the auxiliary problem to find the initial point can be seen as:

div.head: VI. Numerical Results
div.p: The performance of the described approach was evaluated by checking the number of iterations necessary to solve the problem in Phases 1 and 2. To do so, 1000 synthetic task sets with 10, 30 and 50 tasks each were generated using the UUniFast algorithm [17].

Each one of these sets was solved twice with different values of for the Phases 1 and 2. For the experiments it was considered one first case where the value of in Phase 1 was 10 -1 and Phase 2 was 10 -3 , and a second case with values 10 -2 and 10 -6 , respectively. Since the goal of Phase 1 is to find the initial solution, a low tolerance was always given to it.

It is important to mention that the parameters used to solve the problem were not tuned for any set, so better results can be achieved for specific cases by adjusting the parameters. Tuning the parameter for one case can improve the response time for that one, but may degrade the performance for the others. In consequence of the stop criterion in the outer loop and the values of , all sets of tasks of the same scenario were solved with almost the same number of iterations, which implies that a better solution could be found. The large value for implied in fewer iterations in Phase 1.

The Box Plot in Figure 2 shows that the number of outliers are relatively low in Phase 1, and the quartile range, which represents 25% of sample above and below the mean, and the small quartile range and number of outliers indicate low variation. In Phase 2, the number of outliers and the quartile range increased, indicating high variation. But even so most of the sets are solved with less iterations than the average, what indicates that the mean were raised by some instance that took more iterations.

The analysis indicates that: (1) when the number of tasks grows the algorithm becomes more sensitive to the parameters that define the problem instance, as it is illustrated in Box Plot 2 where the number os iterations tends to vary more with 50 tasks than 10 or 30; (2) the mean of the sum of difference between the QoS found for each case with different values of in the sets of 10, 30 and 50 tasks were respectively 7 × 10 -4 , 10 -3 and 38 × 10 -2 ;

(3) the number of iterations to solve the problem did not increase at the same rate of the number of tasks (e.g., when the task set increases from 10 to 50 tasks, 500%, the number of iterations to solve increased 178% ; (4) and a feasible solution can be achieved by solving only Phase 1, with few iterations as is indicated in Table I. But it is important to mention that the solution of Phase 1 is feasible but not the optimal, what implies in less QoS. For example the sets 10, 30 and 50 tasks, solved in the second case achieved a difference of 0.0309, 0.0311 and 0.0286 in QoS between the Phases 1 and 2.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have presented a reconfiguration mechanism for providing energy-savings guarantees in real-time systems. The developed mechanism is based on interior-point methods used as a means of optimizing system QoS subject to both energy and schedulability constraints. Such methods are known to be computationally efficient. The effectiveness of the proposed reconfiguration mechanism was illustrated via a numerical analysis of the algorithm. The relevance of the problem and the effectiveness of the results we found motivate the development of extensions of the proposed reconfiguration mechanism. Future steps of this research include considering tasks with more than one mode of operation and discrete values for CPU frequency.
